67_marg755: Augustine. It is necessary that you be saddened, but where you are saddened, let hope console you. For the most truthful custom of Scripture calls them sleepers for this reason, that when we hear of them sleeping, we may by no means despair that they will awake. There is therefore, for the dead who are loved, a kind of sadness that is in a way natural. For nature shrinks from death, and death would not have befallen man except from preceding guilt. Hence, then, it is necessary that we be sad when those we love leave us in dying, because we also desired that they not leave us forever remaining behind, but go on ahead for a little while and we follow; yet death itself, which nature flees, when it seizes the beloved, saddens in us the affection of that very love.
67_marg756: The same. We are therefore saddened at the deaths of our own by the necessity of losing them, but with the hope of receiving them back. Thence we are afflicted, hence we are consoled. Thence weakness affects us, hence faith restores us. Thence the human condition grieves, hence the divine promise heals. But it may move one how God wept for the dead man who was at once to live at his command. Whence: The Lord wept not for the dead man but for death, which man drew upon himself by sinning. For if sin had not gone before, death without doubt would not have followed. The death of the body therefore followed, which the death of the soul preceded; it preceded by forsaking God, and the death of the body followed when the soul departed. The soul forsook God willingly. It was forced to forsake the body unwillingly. As if it were said to it: You departed from him whom you ought to have loved; depart from him whom you have loved. For who wishes to die? No one at all; and so no one, that it was said to Peter: “Another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldst not.” If there were no bitterness of death, there would surely be no fortitude of martyrs.
67_marg757: As also the rest, etc. Augustine. On the pomp of funerals. Therefore the pomp of the funeral, the costly trains of mourners, the care of burial, the rich construction of monuments, are some kind of comfort to the living, not helps to the dead. But that the dead are helped by the prayers of the holy Church, and by the saving sacrifice, and by the alms which are given for their spirits, is not to be doubted, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins have deserved. For the whole Church observes this, handed down by the fathers: that for those who have died in the communion of the body and blood, prayer is made when at the sacrifice itself they are commemorated in their place, and it is also commemorated that the offering is made for them. And when works of mercy are performed for the sake of commemorating them, who would doubt that he helps those for whom prayers are not offered to God in vain? For it is not to be doubted that these things profit the dead, but such as lived before death in such a way that these things can be useful to them after death. For those who have departed from the body without faith working through love and its sacraments, the offices of this piety are rendered for them by their own in vain, for they lacked the pledge of it while they were here, not treasuring up mercy for themselves but wrath. Therefore new merits are not acquired for the dead when their own do some good for them, but these consequences are rendered to their preceding merits. And so each one, ending this life, cannot have after it anything except what he has merited in it. Let the pious hearts of loved ones therefore be permitted to be saddened by the deaths of their own with a curable grief, and let them shed consolable tears by the mortal condition; yet let the joy of faith restrain these, by which the faithful, when they die, are believed to depart from us for a little while and to pass over to better things. Let there be, according to one’s means, care for burying and building tombs, because in the holy Scriptures these are reckoned among good works, and not only in the bodies of the patriarchs and other saints, but also in the body of the Lord himself, those who did these things are praised. Let men therefore fulfil toward their own the duties of the last service and the soothings of their human grief; but those things which help the spirits of the dead, namely offerings and alms, let them render for them much more carefully and abundantly.
67_marg758: But God could have granted this to believers, that they should not even experience the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain happiness would be added to the flesh, and the strength of faith would be diminished. For men so fear this death that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all; and by this no one would hasten to the grace of Christ for the sake of the future life, but to remove the trouble of death, and thus in a manner softly would men believe in Christ. He has therefore given his faithful more grace. For what great thing is it, seeing that those who believed did not die, to believe that one will not die? How much greater, how much stronger, how much more praiseworthy, to believe in such a way that one who is to die hopes to live without end. Whence also his dear ones who survive can be consoled in the sadness of a friend’s death.

67_marg767: It is commonly asked whether those whom Christ will find alive are never to die at all, or whether at the very moment of time in which they are caught up to meet Christ they will pass over to immortality with wonderful swiftness. For it must not be said that it cannot be that, borne aloft through the air, they die and come to life again in that space; and to this sense, that we should suppose that those whom the Lord will find alive here will, in that small space, both suffer death and receive immortality, the Apostle seems to urge us where he says: “In Christ all shall be made alive.” And elsewhere: “That which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die first.” But why should it seem incredible to us that that multitude of bodies is in a manner sown in the air and there comes to life again immortally and incorruptibly, since we believe that the resurrection will be in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of the most ancient corpses will return into limbs that will live without end, with such ease and such immeasurable swiftness? Nor do we think that those will be exempt from that sentence in which it was said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go,” that is, you will go into this, life lost, which you were before you took life; you will be this, lifeless, which you were before you were enlivened.

For there is a certain measure of good life in which, even in this present conduct, there can be no just complaint. For who justly complains of a man who wishes evil to no one and counsels faithfully those he can, and against the injuries of anyone does not hold the desire of revenge, so that he may truthfully say: “as we also forgive our debtors,” and yet by the very fact that he says this he declares that he is not without sin: “In many things we all offend.”
